title: Verbs that know if you're a man or a woman
title_target: मैं हिंदी बोलती हूँ — maiⁿ hindii boltii huuⁿ
goal: Talk about what you usually do — and face the biggest surprise of Hindi: a verb's form changes with the gender of whoever does the action, including you.
bekal: build sentences in subject – object – verb order
choose -ता, -ती, or -ते to match the subject
negate a sentence with नहीं in the right place
use the twenty most common verbs
describe your daily routine in three sentences

dialogs.title: संवाद — Learning languages, each in our own way
dialogs.intro: Rahul and Ani compare how they learn languages. In line eight Ani notices something that looks trivial, and Rahul explains it in one sentence. That sentence is this whole unit.

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.id: I learn at home, from a book.
lines.literal: I — home — at — learning(fem.) — am, book — from.

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.id: Yes, but I read a little every day.
lines.literal: yes, but — I — every — day — little — reading(fem.) — am.

lines.speaker: राहुल:
lines.id: I study too — English. But I'm very lazy.
lines.literal: I — also — studying(masc.) — am — English. but — I — very — lazy — am.

lines.speaker: राहुल:
lines.id: A little. I understand, but I don't speak.
lines.literal: little. I — understanding(masc.) — am, but — speaking(masc.) — not — am.

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.id: Wait — you say "samajhtaa", and I say "samajhtii"?

lines.speaker: राहुल:
lines.id: Yes! Verbs are boy-and-girl too. I'm a boy, you're a girl.
lines.literal: yes! verb — also — boy–girl — being(fem.) — is. I — boy — am, you — girl — are.

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.id: So a book "speaks-girl" and a room "speaks-boy"?
lines.literal: so — book — "speaking(fem.)" — is — and — room — "speaking(masc.)" — is?

lines.speaker: राहुल:
lines.id: Ha ha! Yes, exactly like that.
lines.literal: ha — ha! yes, completely — like-that — just.

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.id: All right. I understand. I'm learning. I speak!
lines.literal: fine — is. I — understanding(fem.) — am. I — learning(fem.) — am. I — speaking(fem.) — am!

notes: **This unit in one sentence: a Hindi verb changes form with the gender of its subject.** A man says *मैं बोल**ता** हूँ*; a woman says *मैं बोल**ती** हूँ*. Both mean "I speak". ⚠️ This isn't a polite or special form — it's the ordinary form, used in the very first sentence you'll say today. **Decide now which form is yours**, then use it consistently, because the wrong one makes people pause every time.

**The verb is really two words, and both are required.** बोल**ती** + **हूँ**. The first part (*बोलती*) carries gender and number; the second (*हूँ*) carries who the subject is and when it happens. Drop है/हूँ/हैं and the sentence isn't finished — exactly as you learned in unit 1.

**Word order: subject – object – other details – verb.** *मैं हिंदी बोलती हूँ* = "I — Hindi — speaking — am". ⚠️ The verb **always** comes last. That's the opposite of English, and it's the hardest habit to break. One exercise that helps: before you speak, think of the **verb** first, park it at the end, and build the rest in front of it.

**नहीं goes right before the verb.** *मैं बोलती **नहीं** हूँ* or, more commonly in conversation, *मैं **नहीं** बोलती* — with हूँ dropped. ⚠️ Dropping है/हूँ after नहीं is correct and very common, but **only** in habitual sentences like these. For now write it in full; just recognize the short form when you hear it.

**आप takes -ते or -ती, not -ता — even for one person.** आप बोल**ते** हैं (to a man), आप बोल**ती** हैं (to a woman). That follows from the rule in unit 1: respect = plural. **तुम** also takes -ते/-ती, but with हो: *तुम बोलते हो*.

**Things can be subjects too, and the verb follows the thing's gender.** Ani's joke in line 10 is actually true: *गाड़ी चल**ती** है* (the car moves — गाड़ी is feminine), *पानी गिर**ता** है* (water falls — पानी is masculine), *किताबें गिर**ती** हैं* (the books fall). So the noun genders you learned in unit 2 don't stop at adjectives; they seep all the way into the verb.

**आलसी ends in -ी but never changes.** *आलसी लड़का* and *आलसी लड़की* are both correct. Only adjectives ending in **-आ** change form; those ending in -ी, -न, or anything else stay put. Again, good news: the unchanging group is much bigger.

grammars.title: One verb, six forms
body: Drop **-ना** from the dictionary form, add **-ता · -ती · -ते**, then attach the matching form of होना. That's all. The four verbs in this table behave exactly alike, and so do about three hundred other Hindi verbs.
after: ⚠️ Note again that **-ती covers singular and plural at once**. A group of women says *हम बोलती हैं*, just as one woman says *मैं बोलती हूँ*. Only the male side has two forms.
⚠️ If the group is mixed — ten women and one man — Hindi uses the **masculine** form: *वे बोलते हैं*. The rule isn't fair, but that's how it is, and knowing it saves you confusion when you hear it.

grammars.title: The twenty most common verbs
after: ⚠️ **पढ़ना means both "to read" and "to study (at school)".** *मैं किताब पढ़ती हूँ* = I read a book; *मैं स्कूल में पढ़ती हूँ* = I go to school. **सीखना** is for skills: languages, cooking, driving.

sections.title: How often, and describing an ordinary day

blocks.text: These adverbs go before the verb and never change form. Adding just one to your sentence makes it sound far more alive.

blocks.title: Three sentences to describe your ordinary day
items: **मैं रोज़ सात बजे उठती हूँ।** — I get up at seven every day.
**मैं अक्सर घर पर खाना खाती हूँ।** — I often eat at home.
**मैं कभी कभी दोस्तों से मिलती हूँ।** — Sometimes I meet friends.
Swap in a verb from the table on the previous page and an adverb from the table above, and you have twenty different sentences without learning a single new word.

blocks.text: ⚠️ Something to be aware of from now on: **this habitual form is NOT used for things happening right now**. *मैं खाती हूँ* means "I eat (usually)", not "I'm eating". For what's happening at this moment, Hindi has its own form — *मैं खा रही हूँ* — covered in unit 11. Good news for English speakers: it's the same split as *I eat* vs. *I'm eating*, so trust your instinct here.

exercises.prompt: Translate into Hindi. Assume you are a woman.
items: I understand, but I don't speak.

answers: मैं हिंदी नहीं बोलती। — वह यहाँ नहीं रहता। — हम अंग्रेज़ी नहीं समझते। — आप रोज़ नहीं आते।
मैं हिंदी बोलती हूँ। — वह किताब पढ़ता है। — आप कहाँ रहते हैं? — मैं रोज़ सात बजे उठती हूँ। — हम कभी कभी दोस्तों से मिलते हैं।
मैं हर रोज़ हिंदी सीखती हूँ। — मैं समझती हूँ, लेकिन बोलती नहीं हूँ। — वह दिल्ली में रहता है। — हम अक्सर घर पर खाना खाते हैं। — आप कहाँ काम करते हैं? — मैं कभी टीवी नहीं देखती।
